Hands on the wheel

Slides on the left, speaker notes on the right.

<introduce>

I previously worked at Fat Zebra leading a team of a dozen people. Fat Zebra does what Stripe does, but primarily focussed in Australia. I took a redundancy there at the end of August, thinking that finding a new job would take maybe a few weeks. It has not taken “a few weeks”. Changes have had to be made, and I’ve had to compromise on my well crafted resume.

I now have an AI-flavoured version of my resume to widen the possible net for jobs. This is not a serious resume. It’s a piss-take on the current hype around AI. I have almost accidentally sent it out in place of my proper resume. This file is called resume.pdf, which sits next to real-resume.pdf in the same directory.

In this talk, I’m going to cover some skepticism and hope about AI, some existentialism, and then land on a hopeful note about what I think the role of a developer has morphed into.

This absolute abundance of free time “in between” work has led to me doing a lot of reading around what the latest takes are with AI. Both the scathing, like this from Mitchell Hashimoto (read)

Or this graph of CVEs issued. See if you can spot where AI adoption took off.

I’ve not just been hunting for the “AI is bad” takes. I’ve been looking for the good too. I’ve found things like where a researcher may have discovered a new planet by using AI-powered analysis of a huge dataset.

There’s also been some discoveries in fields like Maths and Physics that seem pretty promising too, to this layman.

To be clear: I think there are many good uses of AI out there. There are also bad uses of AI.

When not trawling the internet for the hottest of AI takes, I’ve been interviewing.

I have been getting some interviews with companies. During these interviews, I’m getting a distinct impression that we’re in the middle of the biggest gold rush that we’ve ever seen in tech. Completely eclipsing the fad of blockchains. Everyone’s on board the AI hypetrain. Many C-level execs are getting on the bandwagon because others are. There’s an overwhelming feeling of FOMO — that you don’t want to be the last to be on the AI bandwagon.

This FOMO then filters down through the organisation, with those same execs pushing teams of developers to use AI to accelerate the rate of their development. Have the AI read the card from the Jira board, implement the feature and even ship that feature all the way into production. I have illustrated this flow here for your benefit.

This is legitimately the flow that has been suggested as an acceptable risk to take at a company. This was told to me, with a straight face, by that company’s “AI-Native Staff Engineer”, while he puffed on a vape in the interview room with me. It felt like I was in an episode of Utopia.

These interviews and learning what other companies are like, along with abundance of free time has led me to asking pretty profound questions. You can only call it a proper redundancy if you have days filled with existentialism and self-doubt. It can feel, at times, like my two decades of experience is worth the same as my 107,000 points on Stack Overflow. If you don’t remember what a Stack Overflow is, ask your parents.

On my more optimistic days, I still think there is a place for developers within companies. AI hasn’t eaten the job, just morphed it.

It used to be the case where you could work as a full-stacker, with a really good understanding of either the frontend or the backend and get by with this knowledge. There were then other people who would take on the responsibility and cover your gaps.

Now I’m seeing this role pushed to the two extremes of this graph, into something I’m calling the fuller stack developer. This is someone who can run discovery sessions with customers, translate those sessions into requirements. These requirements should include information about what “done” looks like for this feature, as well as how success is measured on this feature. It should also include observability advice for this work too.

Once those things have been collected, the developer can then put that work through an AI setup. Once the robot has done thinking, the developer then verifies the outcomes of those pieces of software. There might need to be some new infra setup within your Terraform architecture. Maybe some new backend bits and some shiny new frontend.

This verification can take a few different forms. It can be reviewing the code itself, but it really should be focussed on determining if the software does the right thing. Does this piece connect with the rest of the application? Is it useable? Was a bug overlooked?

Once that verification loop has finished successfully, the developer is then responsible for shipping this feature into production.

I suggest this need for developer supervision because we’ve seen cases historically where computers have made horrific mistakes. In 1982, there was a programming error in a machine called the Therac-25, a radiation therapy machine.

From the wikipedia article, there is this quote.

And then there is this quote.

People died.

This was not the only incident.

In 1999, the Post Office company in the UK rolled out new accounting software. This software indicated that hundreds of post offices across the country were committing fraud. In the majority, these post offices were not. It was a software bug.

People were made bankrupt by this. People were sent to jail. 13 suicides were causally linked to this mistake.

You might be thinking: AI does not make mistakes like this.

By their own admissions, in every chat window, ChatGPT and Claude disclose that mistakes can be made by their tools.

I have been trying to use AI as much as I can on my $20/month plan. I’ve been using it to build out my Magic: The Gathering Ruby project. It has made mistakes in here, but nobody has died. Yet.

I set the AI goals of implementing cards in Magic, and let it run. The implementer skill reads the card’s plain text version and works off that.

At the start of this process, I was manually checking the work myself once the implementer ran. I found AI had about a 10-15% failure rate. In most of those cases, it would miss a key part of a card.

In a memorable example, the card implementer implemented abilities 1 and 3 on this card, but missed the middle ability entirely, defining the relevant method as a blank method.

I then evolved the setup to this multi-agent setup. We can now implement sets of cards all at once. The card collector agent runs a process to group cards together into different categories, based on their in-game mechanics.

Then the Implement-set agent tells the card-implementer and card-reviewer agents what to do. The card-reviewer agent reviews the card’s text and compares it with the code & tests for that card. If it detects mistakes, it documents what those mistakes are and passes the work back to the card implementer.

This has reduced the number of mistakes in the implementation of these cards, but it has not eliminated mistakes entirely.

To catch some of the remaining bugs, I’ve made it possible to play these games in the browser. Well, Claude has done this with my prompting. This allows me to see how different cards interact with each other. The game state is then persisted into a database, along with the event logs. When I encounter a bug, I can point the agent at the game’s logs, describe the bug in a few words, and most of the time the card implementer will realise its mistake and fix it. Rarely will I have to prompt it a second time or clarify.

With this approach, I’ve now implemented over two and a half thousand MTG cards, or a little under 10% of the total of all magic cards ever printed. I don’t doubt that a plan larger than the $20/month could feasibly implement the entire collection of all MTG cards ever. While this project isn’t discovering new planets, or pushing the frontier of mathematics along, it is keeping me away from my existentialism.

The role I’ve outlined here is more of a QA role, admittedly. The “business requirements” are clear. As we say when playing Magic: Reading the card, explains the card.

I think that in this modern era of development we should be the steady hands on the wheel of application development. We should be ensuring the quality of the software that the robot writes.

We must also be taking care when the robot is put in charge of making decisions. At Fat Zebra, we had some code that was used to detect card washing attacks, where attackers would use similar card numbers in a short period of time to guess at people’s cards. Before we had this code, we had an alert that would go off and someone would wakeup and stop the attack. Putting code in place meant our developers could sleep better.

At the start of this year, AI got involved in detecting these attacks. It was a simple skill that went something like “read the last X days worth traffic, and detect card washing attacks”. Of course it had some science in there to work out what a card washing attack looked like. We trained it on the known card attacks we had experienced. It caught more of these attacks than the code version did. The AI tools are good at getting meaning from a wealth of data.

The tool would do its analysis and make a suggestion on what action to take: to temporarily disable the account, or to leave it open and tweak some settings, or to do nothing.

A developer at Fat Zebra ran this tool, and the tool helpfully presented data that indicated a pretty severe card washing attempt. An absolutely huge attack. The attack was a series of Commonwealth Bank debit cards, all within a handful of minutes. Thousands of them! The tool presented further data to confirm this, and then made the suggestion that the merchant’s account should be disabled.

The developer then did something utterly amazing. They stepped out of their prompt — unthinkable! — and asked other devs to check the work of the AI agent. The other developers replied and said that nothing should be done about this attack. Nothing at all. People were losing money! The AI tool was indicating that fraud was happening. But why nothing at all?

Nothing got done because of the context that lived in the heads of those developers. This merchant happened to be a large telecommunications company. This company would periodically send batches of several tens of thousands of transactions at scheduled times each day. This AI tool was picking up those transactions and because they matched the criteria enough, the tool determined the right cause of action was to close the account. The Commonwealth bank cards were being flagged because they’re the most commonly issued cards in Australia.

Had the tool made that choice, Fat Zebra would’ve almost surely lost one of its most important accounts.

We cannot trust AI to make decisions that impact our business. We must leave those decisions to humans who have the relevant context.  We can do this in ways outlined by Kunal Bhalla, a developer from the AI startup Thinking Machines.

I’ll quote directly from his article here, as I couldn’t put this into better words than he has.

Observability: Invest heavily in observability, both black-box and white-box, and make sure to keep a direct handle on the metrics instead of solely relying on the agents’ view. As a habit I prefer to triangulate onto a behavior with multiple sources of metrics, and that becomes even more important with systems rapidly becoming opaque. Non-functional requirements: Don’t forget to observe resource utilization and other non-functional requirements: these can be canaries for unexpected behavior. Deterministic validation: Build mechanical straitjackets for the model: have held-out pieces of code or deterministic tools for validation and observations as a hold-out against the model misunderstanding or glitching. Shadow Traffic: Make it possible and cheap to run a deployed candidate against shadow traffic with no side effects: keep it as similar to production as possible, and this can be the final gate to prevent surprises. Style guides: Give the model a style guide based on your existing code and work. I’ve found Claude’s output far more to my taste after having the models generate a style guide based on all the code and blog posts I’ve written in the past. Fast deploys: An often maligned motto at Facebook used to be Move Fast & Break Things: that, too, is an intentional tradeoff to make. If you can’t be sure of quality, make it very easy to deploy code as well – so changes can be shipped and reverted extremely rapidly.

End quote.

None of this advice is new because of AI. It’s old advice. But it’s advice that has now become even more essential with the advancements of AI. We must continue to be the steady hands on the wheel.
